lessons.title: DAW Hardware Components
lessons.description: Computers, peripherals, MIDI controllers, audio interfaces and mixing desks.
lessons.content_html:
Hardware for Digital Audio Workstations

A DAW is a software application for recording, editing and producing music. But the software is only part of the picture — it relies on a range of hardware components to function. This lesson covers every piece of hardware you need to know for the exam.

The Computer

At the centre of any DAW setup is a computer. The key specifications that affect performance are:

  • Operating System (OS) — Windows or macOS. Some DAWs are platform-specific (e.g. Logic Pro is macOS only).
  • RAM (Random Access Memory) — more RAM allows you to run more tracks, plug-ins and virtual instruments simultaneously. 16 GB is a common minimum for music production.
  • Hard drives — SSDs (Solid State Drives) are faster than HDDs (Hard Disk Drives) and reduce load times. Audio projects can be very large, so storage capacity matters.
  • Processor (CPU) — a faster processor handles more real-time audio processing, effects and virtual instruments without stuttering.
  • Display — a large, high-resolution screen makes it easier to work with complex arrangements, mixer views and plug-in interfaces.
Key Fact

The five key computer specifications for DAW work are: operating system, RAM, hard drives (SSD preferred), processor (CPU) and display. Each affects performance, speed and workflow.

Peripherals

Peripherals are external devices that connect to the computer to extend its capabilities.

  • External storage — USB drives, external SSDs, cloud storage and network drives provide additional space for backing up projects and storing sample libraries.
  • Data input devices — keyboard, mouse, trackpad and touchscreen are used to navigate the DAW, edit MIDI, draw automation and control parameters.
  • Audio output — studio monitors (speakers) and headphones are essential for hearing the audio accurately. Studio monitors are designed for flat, uncoloured playback so you can make reliable mixing decisions.
  • Portable devices — tablets and smartphones can control DAW functions remotely or run lightweight music apps.

MIDI Controllers

MIDI controllers are hardware devices that send MIDI data to the DAW. They don’t produce sound themselves — they trigger sounds in software instruments. Types include:

  • Keyboard controllers — piano-style keys for playing melodies, chords and bass lines.
  • Guitar controllers — guitar-shaped devices that send MIDI from string input.
  • Percussion controllers — pads that are struck like drums to trigger samples and beats.
  • Wind controllers — blown like woodwind instruments to control breath-sensitive virtual instruments.
  • Control surfaces — devices with faders, knobs, pads and data wheels that mimic a mixing desk for hands-on control. DJ controllers include jog wheels, crossfaders and performance pads for live mixing.

An audio interface is the bridge between the analogue world of microphones and instruments and the digital world of the DAW. It converts analogue signals to digital (for recording) and digital signals to analogue (for playback through speakers or headphones).

Input types:

  • Line inputs — accept signals from devices like keyboards, drum machines and playback equipment. Connector types include RCA phono, quarter-inch jack, mini jack and stereo quarter-inch jack.
  • Microphone inputs — accept signals from microphones via XLR, USB or quarter-inch connectors.
  • Instrument input (DI) — a DI (Direct Input) designed for instruments like electric guitar and bass, which have high-impedance signals.

Output types: Audio interfaces provide both balanced and unbalanced outputs. Balanced outputs use three conductors to cancel electrical noise, making them essential for professional studio monitors.

Interfaces also provide phantom power (+48V) to power condenser microphones and gain control to adjust the input signal level.

A MIDI interface connects MIDI devices to a computer. It has three port types: IN (receives data from a controller), OUT (sends data to a sound module) and THRU (passes through received data to chain devices). Connectors are typically 5-pin DIN or USB.

A mixing desk (also called a mixer or mixing console) combines and processes multiple audio signals. Mixing desks come in three architectures:

  • Analogue — processes audio entirely in the analogue domain using physical circuits.
  • Digital — converts audio to digital and processes it using DSP (Digital Signal Processing).
  • Hybrid — combines analogue signal paths with digital control and recall.

A mixing desk provides audio inputs and outputs, can serve as a DAW interface (sending audio to and from the computer) and doubles as a control surface with physical faders and knobs.

Key Fact

A MIDI interface has three ports: IN (receives data), OUT (sends data) and THRU (passes data through to chain devices). Connectors are 5-pin DIN or USB.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Hardware questions often test whether you can identify the correct connector or device for a given scenario. For example, “What type of input would you use to connect an electric guitar directly to an audio interface?” (Answer: DI/instrument input). Learn the connector types (XLR for mics, quarter-inch for line/instruments, RCA for consumer audio, DIN for MIDI) and match them to their uses.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A DAW computer needs adequate RAM, a fast CPU, SSD storage and a good display.
  • MIDI controllers (keyboard, guitar, percussion, wind, control surface) send data to trigger software instruments — they don’t produce sound.
  • An audio interface converts between analogue and digital signals. Key features include line/mic/DI inputs, balanced outputs, phantom power and gain control.

lessons.title: DAW Software Functions
lessons.description: Project setup, track types, software instruments, editing, automation and plug-ins.
lessons.content_html:
Working Inside a DAW

Once your hardware is set up, the real work happens inside the DAW software. This lesson covers the key software functions you need to know: project configuration, track types, software instruments, editing, automation, processing plug-ins and exporting.

DAW Types & Project Configuration

DAWs come in two main types: cloud-based (run in a web browser, e.g. BandLab, Soundtrap) and desktop (installed on your computer, e.g. Logic Pro, Ableton Live, FL Studio). Desktop DAWs generally offer more features and processing power.

When starting a new project, you must configure several settings:

  • Opening or creating a project — start from scratch or use a template with tracks and instruments pre-loaded.
  • Bit depth — determines the dynamic range of the audio. 16-bit is CD quality; 24-bit is standard for professional recording because it captures a wider dynamic range.
  • Sample rate — the number of audio snapshots taken per second. 44.1 kHz is CD quality; 48 kHz and 96 kHz offer higher fidelity. Higher sample rates create larger files.
  • Buffer size — controls how much audio data is held in memory before processing. A small buffer is best for recording (low latency — minimal delay) while a larger buffer is better for mixing (stable processing, fewer glitches).
  • Folders, saving and shortcuts — organise projects into folders, save regularly, and use keyboard shortcuts (copy, paste, cut, save, undo) for efficient workflow.
  • Tempo and time signature — set the BPM (beats per minute) and time signature (e.g. 4/4, 3/4) to match the music.
Key Fact

Buffer size controls the trade-off between latency and stability. Use a small buffer when recording (low latency so the performer hears themselves in real time) and a larger buffer when mixing (stable processing with more plug-ins).

Track Types

DAWs offer three main track types:

  • Audio tracks — record and play back audio signals. You set the input (which interface channel) and output (where the sound goes), and choose mono (one channel, e.g. a single mic) or stereo (two channels, e.g. a keyboard).
  • Software instrument tracks — host virtual instruments inside the DAW. You play them via MIDI and the software generates the audio.
  • MIDI tracks — record and play MIDI data that is routed to external hardware instruments or internal software instruments. You set the MIDI input (controller) and output (destination instrument).

Software instruments fall into two categories: synth presets (pre-made sounds from virtual synthesisers) and sampler presets (recorded audio samples mapped across a keyboard). Synth editing allows you to adjust the envelope (attack, decay, sustain, release), filter (brightness/darkness) and waveform (the basic shape of the sound). Sampler editing lets you import samples, map them to different keys and set loop points.

Loops are pre-recorded audio or MIDI patterns designed to repeat seamlessly. Audio loops are fixed recordings, while MIDI loops can be edited (change notes, tempo, instruments). Loops speed up production by providing ready-made rhythms, bass lines and melodies.

Editing

Editing is where you shape and refine your recordings. The DAW provides separate editing tools for MIDI and audio.

MIDI editing: You view notes on a pitch/rhythm grid (piano roll) and can cut, copy, paste and move them freely. Quantise snaps notes to the grid to correct timing — with options for swing (a subtle rhythmic groove) and humanisation (small random variations to avoid a mechanical feel). You can also edit velocity (how hard a note is played), pitch bend and controller data (e.g. modulation wheel, sustain pedal).

Audio editing: Key operations include trim (cutting unwanted sections), copy and paste, reverse (playing audio backwards), time stretch (changing length without affecting pitch) and pitch manipulation (changing pitch without affecting length).

Automation

Automation lets you record changes to parameters over time. Instead of manually adjusting a fader during playback, you draw or record the movement and the DAW replays it automatically. You can automate volume, pan (left/right positioning), instrument parameters and plug-in parameters (e.g. filter cutoff, reverb level).

Processing Plug-ins

Plug-ins are software effects that process audio in real time. The main categories are:

  • Effects — reverb (simulates room reflections) and delay (repeats the signal after a time gap).
  • Modulation — chorus (thickens sound by layering slightly detuned copies), flanging (sweeping comb filter) and phasing (shifting phase relationship).
  • Filter — wah-wah (sweeps a bandpass filter for an expressive effect).
  • Distortion — amp simulation (models guitar amplifiers) and overdrive (warm, mild clipping).
  • EQ — adjusts specific frequency bands. Controls include low/high pass filters, frequency selection, Q (bandwidth), gain and attenuation.
  • Dynamics — compressor (reduces dynamic range), limiter (prevents signal exceeding a threshold) and gate (silences audio below a threshold). Key parameters: threshold, ratio, attack, release and gain.
Key Fact

A compressor’s four key parameters are: threshold (the level above which compression starts), ratio (how much the signal is reduced), attack (how quickly compression kicks in) and release (how quickly it stops). Gain compensates for volume lost during compression.

Exporting

When a project is complete, you export (also called “bounce”) it to a stereo audio file. You can export the entire project or individual parts. Export settings include bit depth, sample rate and file format: WAV and AIF are uncompressed (high quality, large files), while MP3 is compressed (smaller file, some quality loss).
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers a lot of terminology. In the exam, you may be asked to describe a specific function (e.g. “Describe what quantise does in a DAW”) or explain why a setting matters (e.g. “Explain why buffer size is important when recording”). Always give the function AND its purpose or effect. For plug-in questions, know the difference between EQ (frequency), dynamics (volume) and modulation (time-based) effects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Configure projects with the right bit depth, sample rate, buffer size, tempo and time signature before recording.
  • MIDI editing uses quantise, velocity and pitch bend; audio editing uses trim, time stretch and pitch manipulation.
  • Processing plug-ins include effects (reverb, delay), modulation (chorus, flanger, phaser), EQ, dynamics (compressor, limiter, gate) and distortion.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a producer would use automation in a mix.
practice_questions.marks: Automation records parameter changes over time so the DAW plays them back automatically (1). This means volume, pan and effects can change dynamically throughout a song without manual adjustment during playback (1). For example, a producer could automate volume to create a gradual fade-out or automate reverb to increase during a chorus (1). This gives precise, repeatable control over the mix and creates more dynamic, professional-sounding productions (1). 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the role of processing plug-ins in shaping the final sound of a music production.

Indicative content: EQ shapes the tonal balance (boost/cut frequencies, remove muddiness, add clarity); dynamics processing (compressor controls dynamic range for consistency, limiter prevents clipping, gate removes unwanted noise); reverb/delay add spatial depth and ambience; modulation adds movement and texture; distortion adds character and energy. Credit examples of specific use cases and how plug-ins work together in a mix chain.

practice_questions.text: A student has recorded a MIDI keyboard performance that has some timing errors and the volume levels are uneven. Discuss the DAW tools and techniques they could use to improve the performance.
practice_questions.marks:

Lower band (1-2): Limited identification.
Indicative content: Timing — quantise to snap notes to grid, with swing or humanisation to maintain natural feel; manual note editing on piano roll to move/delete specific notes. Volume — edit velocity values for individual notes; apply compression plug-in to even out dynamic range; use automation to control volume changes over time. Additional refinement: adjust note lengths, correct wrong pitches on the grid, add pitch bend or modulation data. Export settings for final output.

lessons.title: Creating Audio with a DAW & Health and Safety
lessons.description: Applied DAW workflow from project setup to export, plus studio health and safety.
lessons.content_html:
Putting It All Together

This lesson brings together everything from the previous two lessons into a practical workflow. You will learn how to set up a project, capture audio and MIDI, edit and refine your work, and export a finished stereo mix. The second half covers the health and safety considerations that apply in any studio environment.

Applied DAW Workflow

Step 1: Project Configuration

Start by creating a new project. Set the bit depth (24-bit for professional quality), sample rate (44.1 kHz or 48 kHz depending on the destination), and configure the audio output to route sound to your monitors or headphones via the audio interface. Set the tempo (BPM) and time signature to match the piece you are creating. Organise your project with clearly named folders, and save the project immediately. Use keyboard shortcuts (copy, paste, cut, save, undo) throughout to speed up your workflow.

Step 2: Capturing Audio & MIDI

There are several ways to get sound into your project:

  • Audio tracks — create audio tracks and record live instruments or vocals through the audio interface. Select the correct input channel, set the gain level to avoid clipping, and arm the track for recording.
  • Importing audio — drag existing audio files (WAV, AIF, MP3) directly into the timeline.
  • Recording via interface — select the input on your audio interface, adjust the gain so the signal is strong but not distorting, and press record.
  • Importing MIDI — load pre-made MIDI files into MIDI or software instrument tracks.
  • MIDI controller input — play a MIDI keyboard or percussion controller to record performance data in real time.
  • MIDI programming — use the mouse, trackpad or DAW edit pages (piano roll) to draw MIDI notes directly onto the grid.
Key Fact

Six methods of capturing audio and MIDI: recording audio tracks, importing audio files, recording via the interface with correct gain, importing MIDI files, MIDI controller input (real-time performance) and MIDI programming (drawing notes on the grid).

Step 3: Editing & Refining

Once captured, use DAW tools to shape your material:

  • Software instruments — assign virtual instruments to software instrument tracks and adjust their settings (synth presets, sampler presets, envelope, filter, waveform).
  • Loops — browse and add audio or MIDI loops to fill out your arrangement.
  • Editing tools — trim, copy, paste, quantise, adjust velocity, time stretch and pitch manipulate as needed.
  • Processing plug-ins — apply EQ, compression, reverb, delay and other effects to shape the tone, dynamics and space of each track.

When the mix is complete, export the project as a stereo mixdown. Choose the appropriate bit depth, sample rate and file format. WAV or AIF for high-quality masters; MP3 for sharing online or streaming. You can also export individual parts (stems) for further processing or remixing.

Health & Safety in the Studio

Studios contain electrical equipment, cables and screens that present real risks. The spec requires you to know about hazards, risks, risk assessment and control measures.

Hazards & Risks

A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm. A risk is the likelihood that the hazard will cause harm and how severe that harm could be.

The four main studio hazards and their associated risks are:

  • Noise — prolonged exposure to loud sound through monitors or headphones can cause hearing loss, which is often permanent and irreversible.
  • Displays — staring at computer screens for extended periods causes eye strain, headaches and fatigue.
  • Slip, trip and fall hazards — cables running across the floor, equipment cases and cluttered spaces can cause falls, resulting in back pain, sprains or fractures.
  • Electrical hazards — faulty wiring, overloaded sockets and damaged cables can cause electrocution, burns or fire.
Key Fact

Four studio hazards and their risks: noise (hearing loss), displays (eye strain), slip/trip/fall (back pain, sprains), electrical (electrocution). You must be able to identify hazards AND explain the associated risks.

Risk Assessment & Control Measures

A risk assessment is a formal process of identifying hazards, evaluating how likely they are to cause harm and deciding what control measures to put in place.

Common control measures in a studio include:

  • Noise — limit listening levels, take regular breaks, use noise-limiting headphones.
  • Displays — position screens at eye level, adjust brightness, take regular screen breaks (20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds).
  • Slip/trip/fall — use cable management (cable ties, trunking, gaffer tape), keep walkways clear, store equipment properly.
  • Electrical — PAT test equipment regularly, avoid overloading sockets, replace damaged cables, use RCDs (residual current devices).

Reporting: Any hazards, incidents or near-misses must be reported to a supervisor or health and safety officer. Accurate reporting helps prevent future incidents.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Health and safety questions are common in this exam. You may be asked to identify hazards in a given studio scenario, explain associated risks or suggest control measures. Always match each hazard to its specific risk — e.g. “The trailing cable is a trip hazard (hazard) that could cause a fall resulting in a sprain or back injury (risk).” For the DAW workflow section, practise describing the steps in order: configure, capture, edit, export.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The DAW workflow follows four steps: project configuration, capture (audio and MIDI), editing and refining, and export to stereo.
  • Studio hazards include noise, displays, slip/trip/fall and electrical — each has specific risks and control measures.
  • Risk assessments identify hazards, evaluate risks and determine control measures. All incidents must be reported.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a control measure for reducing the risk of hearing loss in a studio?
A) Using cable trunking
B) Limiting listening levels and taking regular breaks
C) Adjusting screen brightness
D) PAT testing equipment
practice_questions.marks: B — Limiting listening levels and taking regular breaks (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways of inputting MIDI data into a DAW project.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: importing MIDI files (1), playing a MIDI controller in real time (1), programming notes using the mouse/trackpad on the piano roll (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of recording audio through an audio interface into a DAW.
practice_questions.marks: Select the correct input on the audio interface (1). Set the gain level so the signal is strong but not clipping/distorting (1). Create an audio track in the DAW, arm it for recording and press record (1). 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important to carry out a risk assessment before using a recording studio.
practice_questions.marks: A risk assessment identifies potential hazards in the studio environment (1). It evaluates how likely each hazard is to cause harm and how severe that harm could be (1). Control measures are then put in place to reduce or eliminate the risks (1). This protects the health and safety of everyone using the studio and meets legal requirements (1). 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the importance of correct project configuration settings (bit depth, sample rate, buffer size) when starting a new DAW project.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed analysis of all three settings with clear explanation of their impact.
Mid band (3-4): Sound analysis of at least two settings.
Lower band (1-2): Basic identification.
Indicative content: Bit depth — 24-bit captures wider dynamic range than 16-bit, reducing quantisation noise; if set too low, recordings lose detail. Sample rate — higher rates (48/96 kHz) capture more frequency detail but create larger files; must match the target format. Buffer size — small for recording (low latency) so performers hear themselves in real time; large for mixing (stable processing with more plug-ins). Incorrect settings can cause poor quality recordings, latency issues during performance, or system instability.

practice_questions.text: A school music studio has been set up with new equipment. Discuss the health and safety considerations that should be addressed before students begin using the space, and explain the control measures that should be put in place.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive discussion covering all four hazard types with appropriate control measures and a systematic approach to risk assessment.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good coverage of multiple hazards with relevant control measures.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some hazards identified with basic measures.
Lower band (1-2): Limited response.
Indicative content: Conduct a risk assessment before use. Noise — set maximum volume levels on monitors and headphones, limit session lengths, provide breaks. Displays — position screens correctly, adjust brightness, enforce screen breaks. Cables/equipment — use cable management to prevent trips, keep walkways clear, store equipment when not in use. Electrical — PAT test all equipment, check cables for damage, avoid overloading sockets, use RCDs. Reporting — establish a system for reporting hazards and incidents. Student induction/training on safe use of equipment.
